items.title: Quiz Q#637 · Wilfred Owen
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Wilfred Owen
items.stem: Which searing World War I poem by Wilfred Owen depicts a gas attack on retreating British soldiers and repudiates the patriotic claim from Horace that 'it is sweet and honorable to die for one's country' as 'the old Lie'?
items.explanation: Wilfred Owen's 'Dulce et Decorum Est' (composed 1917, published 1920) is the definitive anti-war lyric exposing the horrific realities of trench warfare.

items.title: Quiz Q#638 · Wilfred Owen
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Wilfred Owen
items.stem: In which work by Wilfred Owen does the character The soldier speaker (The voice in many of the war poems, often a man in the trenches) appear?
items.explanation: The soldier speaker (The voice in many of the war poems, often a man in the trenches) is a central character in Wilfred Owen's Poems.

items.title: Quiz Q#639 · Wilfred Owen
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Wilfred Owen
items.stem: Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line: "The Poetry is in the pity."?
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Wilfred Owen's Poems.

items.title: Quiz Q#640 · Wilfred Owen
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Wilfred Owen
items.stem:
Which of the following works by Wilfred Owen matches this literary feature / description?
"That year is wrong for this book. Chatto and Windus published Poems in London in 1920. The preface line about pity belongs to a draft Owen wrote for a book he did not live to see. Blunden's 1931 edition is not the first book."
items.explanation: That year is wrong for this book. Chatto and Windus published Poems in London in 1920. The preface line about pity belongs to a draft Owen wrote for a book he did not live to see. Blunden's 1931 edition is not the first book. describes Poems (1920) by Wilfred Owen.

items.title: Quiz Q#641 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: In James Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, which medieval philosopher's aesthetic principles (integritas, consonantia, claritas) does Stephen Dedalus adapt to formulate his theory of art?
items.explanation: In Chapter 5 of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Stephen Dedalus expounds his neo-Thomist aesthetic theory based on St. Thomas Aquinas's criteria of beauty: integritas (wholeness), consonantia (harmony), and claritas (radiance).

items.title: Quiz Q#642 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: Which landmark modernist novel begins with the famous childhood memory: 'Once upon a time and a very good time it was there was a moocow coming down along the road and this moocow that was coming down along the road met a nicens little boy named baby tuckoo'?
options: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
items.explanation: James Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) opens with this famous stylistic mimicry of an infant's sensory and linguistic development.

items.title: Quiz Q#643 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: In A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, which Latin phrase does Stephen Dedalus adopt as his defiant motto of rebellion against church, family, and nation?
items.explanation: Stephen Dedalus declares 'Non serviam' ('I will not serve that in which I no longer believe'), echoing Lucifer's rebellion to affirm his commitment to artistic freedom.

items.title: Quiz Q#644 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: At the conclusion of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Stephen Dedalus vows to go forth into exile to encounter the reality of experience and to:
options: die for the national resurrection of Catholic Ireland
seek the holy grail of ancient Celtic wisdom
forge in the smithy of my soul the uncreated conscience of my race
reconcile the dogmas of the Church with classical philosophy
items.explanation: In his diary entry on 26 April, Stephen concludes with this iconic manifesto of modern artistic purpose, invoking his mythic namesake Daedalus: 'the great artificer'.

items.title: Quiz Q#645 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: Which celebrated modernist novel opens on the morning of 16 June 1904 with the line: 'Stately, plump Buck Mulligan came from the stairhead, bearing a bowl of lather on which a mirror and a razor lay crossed'?
items.explanation: James Joyce's Ulysses (1922) begins atop the Martello Tower in Sandycove with Buck Mulligan performing a mock-liturgical shaving ritual in the Telemachus episode.

items.title: Quiz Q#646 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: In James Joyce's Ulysses, who represents the Telemachus figure corresponding to Homer's Odyssey in the opening three episodes of the novel?
items.explanation: In Joyce's Homeric schema, the young dispossessed intellectual Stephen Dedalus corresponds to Prince Telemachus searching for a spiritual father.

items.title: Quiz Q#647 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: In which episode of Ulysses is the protagonist Leopold Bloom introduced preparing breakfast and relishing 'the inner organs of beasts and fowls'?
items.explanation: Episode 4 ('Calypso') introduces Leopold Bloom at 8 Eccles Street, famously cooking a mutton kidney for breakfast.

items.title: Quiz Q#648 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: Under which pseudonymous alter-ego does Leopold Bloom conduct his secret romantic correspondence with Martha Clifford in the Lotus Eaters episode of Ulysses?
items.explanation: In Episode 5 ('Lotus Eaters'), Bloom picks up a clandestine letter at the Westland Row post office addressed to his pseudonym 'Henry Flower'.

items.title: Quiz Q#649 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: In the Hades episode (Episode 6) of James Joyce's Ulysses, where do Leopold Bloom, Simon Dedalus, and their acquaintances travel in a carriage for Paddy Dignam's funeral?
items.explanation: Episode 6 ('Hades') corresponds to Odysseus's descent into the Underworld, as Bloom and companions travel through Dublin to Glasnevin Cemetery.

items.title: Quiz Q#650 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: Which episode of Ulysses is set in the Freeman's Journal newspaper offices and is famously structured with over sixty sensationalized rhetorical newspaper headlines?
items.explanation: Episode 7 ('Aeolus') takes place amid printing presses and editor windbags, punctuated throughout with mock-heroic and journalistic headlines.

items.title: Quiz Q#651 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: In which episode of Ulysses does James Joyce construct the prose according to the musical form of an eight-part fugue (fuga per canonem) in the Ormond Hotel bar?
items.explanation: Episode 11 ('Sirens') uses sound associations, onomatopoeia, and polyphonic wordplay to recreate the acoustic textures and musical fugue of the Sirens.

items.title: Quiz Q#652 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: In the Cyclops episode (Episode 12) of Ulysses, who represents the one-eyed, xenophobic Homeric giant who throws a biscuit tin at Leopold Bloom?
items.explanation: The Cyclops episode satirizes aggressive anti-Semitic Irish nationalism through 'The Citizen', modeled in part on GAA founder Michael Cusack.

items.title: Quiz Q#653 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: Which episode of Ulysses employs the breathless, sentimental idiom of late-Victorian women's fashion magazines and pulp romances to narrate Gerty MacDowell's encounter with Bloom on Sandymount Strand?
items.explanation: Episode 13 ('Nausicaa') parodies consumerist romantic fiction through Gerty MacDowell's point of view before shifting back to Bloom's realist monologue.

items.title: Quiz Q#654 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: Which tour de force episode of Ulysses chronicles the nine-month gestation of language by parodying the chronological evolution of English prose style from Anglo-Saxon alliterative verse to modern slang?
items.explanation: Episode 14 ('Oxen of the Sun'), set in the Holles Street maternity hospital, traces historical English prose styles through thirty-two chronological parodies alongside the birth of Mina Purefoy's child.

items.title: Quiz Q#655 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: Which episode of Ulysses, set in Nighttown (the Dublin red-light district), is written in the form of an expressionist theatrical script where characters' subconscious guilts and hallucinations come alive?
items.explanation: Episode 15 ('Circe') is an immense hallucinatory drama set in Bella Cohen's brothel where Bloom and Stephen confront their deepest psychological fears and fantasies.

items.title: Quiz Q#656 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: Which episode of Ulysses was described by James Joyce as his personal favorite, written in the style of an objective, impersonal scientific catechism with 309 questions and answers?
items.explanation: Episode 17 ('Ithaca') presents Bloom and Stephen's return to 8 Eccles Street in cold, encyclopedic, mathematical Q&A form before Stephen departs into the night.

items.title: Quiz Q#657 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: How many unpunctuated sentences make up Molly Bloom's famous closing stream of consciousness monologue in the 'Penelope' episode of Ulysses?
items.explanation: Molly Bloom's 40-page interior monologue in 'Penelope' (Episode 18) consists of eight giant unpunctuated sentences culminating in her passionate affirmation of life: 'yes I said yes I will Yes'.

items.title: Quiz Q#658 · James Joyce
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · James Joyce
items.stem: Which pioneering modernist work begins and ends mid-sentence with the circular flow of the River Liffey, opening with 'riverrun, past Eve and Adam's, from swerve of shore to bend of bay'?
items.explanation: James Joyce's Finnegans Wake (1939) is constructed as a cyclical night-dream using multi-lingual portmanteau words, ending mid-sentence with 'A way a lone a last a loved a long the' which loops directly back into 'riverrun'.

items.title: Quiz Q#659 · Joseph Conrad
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: Where is the cruising yawl Nellie anchored when Charles Marlow begins narrating his journey to the Congo in Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness?
options: On the River Thames at Gravesend
items.explanation: Heart of Darkness uses a frame narrative opening on the cruising yawl Nellie anchored in the Thames estuary at Gravesend as evening falls over London.

items.title: Quiz Q#660 · Joseph Conrad
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: In the opening pages of Heart of Darkness, Charles Marlow startles his companions aboard the Nellie by remarking about England:
options: 'Here stands the beacon of Christian enlightenment.'
'The empire upon which the sun never sets.'
'And this also has been one of the dark places of the earth.'
'Only the sea can forgive the sins of conquerors.'
items.explanation: Marlow reflects that when the Roman legionnaires first sailed up the Thames, Britain itself was a savage wilderness comparable to central Africa.

items.title: Quiz Q#661 · Joseph Conrad
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: In Heart of Darkness, whom does Marlow encounter guarding the door at the Company's European headquarters in the 'sepulchral city'?
options: An ivory broker counting ledger sheets
items.explanation: The two women knitting black wool like the mythic Fates (Moirae) symbolize foreboding doom and indifferent destiny at the threshold of the colonial enterprise.

items.title: Quiz Q#662 · Joseph Conrad
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: What horrifying handwritten postscript did Kurtz scrawl at the end of his eloquent report for the International Society for the Suppression of Savage Customs?
items.explanation: Kurtz's idealistic humanitarian rhetoric unravels completely into genocidal savagery with this scrawled postscript at the bottom of the page.

items.title: Quiz Q#663 · Joseph Conrad
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: What are the final dying words whispered by the ivory agent Kurtz in Heart of Darkness as he looks into the abyss of his soul?
items.explanation: Kurtz's deathbed declaration—'The horror! The horror!'—stands as one of modern literature's most iconic judgments on moral corruption and imperial greed.

items.title: Quiz Q#664 · Joseph Conrad
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: When Marlow visits Kurtz's grieving fiancée ('the Intended') in the sepulchral city at the end of Heart of Darkness, what does he tell her was Kurtz's last word?
items.explanation: To preserve the Intended's illusion and protect her from the darkness, Marlow lies, telling her that Kurtz's last utterance on his deathbed was her name.

items.title: Quiz Q#665 · Joseph Conrad
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: In Joseph Conrad's Lord Jim, what disgraceful act haunts the protagonist Jim throughout his entire subsequent life?
options: Stealing gold from a native chieftain in Sumatra
Killing a fellow officer during a violent typhoon
Mutinying against the captain of the Sephora
Abandoning the damaged pilgrim ship SS Patna and its 800 passengers
items.explanation: Jim leaps into a lifeboat believing the damaged ship SS Patna will immediately sink with 800 Muslim pilgrims aboard, destroying his romantic ideal of heroic conduct.

items.title: Quiz Q#666 · Joseph Conrad
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: In Lord Jim, where does Jim finally earn redemption, peace, and the reverent title 'Tuan Jim' before catastrophe strikes?
items.explanation: With the merchant Stein's help, Jim retreats to isolated Patusan in the Malay Archipelago, becoming the trusted protector of the local Bugis community.

items.title: Quiz Q#667 · Joseph Conrad
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: In which fictional South American country is Joseph Conrad's epic political masterpiece Nostromo (1904) set?
items.explanation: Conrad invented the complex, turbulent republic of Costaguana (centered on the port of Sulaco) to explore imperialism, political revolution, and capitalism.

items.title: Quiz Q#668 · Joseph Conrad
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: What material commodity forms the corrupting, omnipresent symbol of wealth and power at the heart of Conrad's Nostromo?
options: The rubber of the tropical interior
The silver of the San Tomé mine
The oil fields of Golfo Placido
items.explanation: The San Tomé silver mine, reopened by Charles Gould, becomes an incorruptible yet devastating force that warps the lives of all who touch it.

items.title: Quiz Q#669 · Joseph Conrad
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: Which London landmark is targeted for an anarchist bomb explosion by Mr. Vladimir in Joseph Conrad's political thriller The Secret Agent (1907)?
items.explanation: Mr. Vladimir orders an assault on pure science—the Greenwich Observatory (the meridian of Greenwich)—to shock the British bourgeois public into repressive laws.

items.title: Quiz Q#670 · Joseph Conrad
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: In the famous Preface to which 1897 work did Joseph Conrad define his artistic aim: 'by the power of the written word to make you hear, to make you feel—it is, before all, to make you see'?
items.explanation: Conrad's 1897 Preface to The Nigger of the 'Narcissus' is a cornerstone modernist aesthetic manifesto proclaiming the sensory and emotional mission of fiction.

items.title: Quiz Q#671 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: Which philosophical concept did George Bernard Shaw expound in Man and Superman as the creative, evolutionary biological drive seeking higher self-awareness?
items.explanation: Shaw's concept of the 'Life Force' posits a vital evolutionary impulse working through humanity, specifically through women pursuing men to breed the Superman.

items.title: Quiz Q#672 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: Which famous extended philosophical dream interlude in Act III of George Bernard Shaw's Man and Superman features a philosophical debate between Don Juan, Doña Ana, the Statue, and the Devil?
items.explanation: 'Don Juan in Hell' is often performed as an independent two-hour philosophical debate contrasting the illusion of heavenly purpose with the pleasure-seeking of hell.

items.title: Quiz Q#673 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: Which radical ideological document is appended to George Bernard Shaw's published text of Man and Superman under the authorship of protagonist John Tanner?
items.explanation: Shaw included 'The Revolutionist's Handbook and Pocket Companion' by John Tanner, M.I.R.C., presenting biting aphorisms and eugenic theories on human progress.

items.title: Quiz Q#674 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: In George Bernard Shaw's Major Barbara, what does the arms industrialist Andrew Undershaft identify as the greatest and only real crime of modern civilization?
items.explanation: Undershaft scandalizes his Salvation Army daughter Barbara by arguing that poverty is the mother of all crimes, and that money and gunpowder are the true foundations of morality.

items.title: Quiz Q#675 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: Which character in Major Barbara, a Greek scholar engaged to Barbara Undershaft, agrees to take over the Undershaft munitions business by proving he is a foundling?
items.explanation: Adolphus Cusins (modeled on the real-life Oxford classical scholar Gilbert Murray) decides to use the power of weapons to arm society against oppression.

items.title: Quiz Q#676 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: Where does the opening scene of George Bernard Shaw's Pygmalion (1913) take place as pedestrians take shelter from torrential rain?
options: Outside Higgins's laboratory on Wimpole Street
Under the portico of St. Paul's Church, Covent Garden
At the flower stalls of Piccadilly Circus
items.explanation: Act I opens under the church portico in Covent Garden where Professor Henry Higgins demonstrates his phonetic ability to identify anyone's birthplace by dialect.

items.title: Quiz Q#677 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: Which shocking colloquial phrase, uttered by Eliza Doolittle at Mrs. Higgins's high-society at-home tea party, became a sensational catchphrase in Edwardian London?
items.explanation: Eliza's transition from phonetic correctness into Cockney slang culminated in the line 'Not bloody likely!', which caused an enormous scandal and delight at its 1914 premiere.

items.title: Quiz Q#678 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: In Pygmalion, what social category does Eliza's dustman father, Alfred Doolittle, proudly claim to belong to before becoming burdened by unexpected wealth?
items.explanation: Alfred Doolittle delivers a brilliant comic defense of the 'undeserving poor', who have the same appetites as the deserving poor without bourgeois moral restrictions.

items.title: Quiz Q#679 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: Which 1923 historical masterpiece by George Bernard Shaw dramatizes the trial, condemnation, and posthumous rehabilitation of Joan of Arc, concluding with an epilogue in 1456?
items.explanation: Saint Joan earned Shaw international acclaim and contributed directly to his 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature, presenting Joan as an early nationalist and Protestant martyr.

items.title: Quiz Q#680 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: In the Epilogue to Saint Joan, when Joan asks if she should rise from the dead and return as a living woman, how do the kings, bishops, and executioners react?
options: They fall to their knees and welcome her back with open arms
They demand that she be burnt at the stake a second time
They all make hurried excuses and desert her one by one
They crown her as the eternal queen of France
items.explanation: The play ends on Joan's tragic lament: 'O God that madest this beautiful earth, when will it be ready to receive Thy saints? How long, O Lord, how long?'.

items.title: Quiz Q#681 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: How did George Bernard Shaw divide his two 1898 collections of early dramas confronting contemporary Victorian social problems?
options: Plays for Puritans and Plays for Pagans
items.explanation: Plays Unpleasant included Widowers' Houses (slum landlordism) and Mrs. Warren's Profession (prostitution), while Plays Pleasant included Arms and the Man and Candida.

items.title: Quiz Q#682 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: In George Bernard Shaw's Arms and the Man (1894), which practical Swiss mercenary soldier punctures Raina's romantic notions of military heroism by carrying chocolate cream instead of cartridges?
items.explanation: Captain Bluntschli is the quintessential Shavian realist, exposing romantic military valor as suicidal posturing.

items.title: Quiz Q#683 · J. M. Synge
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · J. M. Synge
items.stem: Which famous word spoken by Christy Mahon regarding female undergarments provoked audience riots during the 1907 premiere of The Playboy of the Western World at the Abbey Theatre?
items.explanation: Dublin audiences were outraged by the word 'shift' (a woman's slip) and the play's perceived slander against Irish peasant morality, igniting week-long Abbey Theatre riots.

items.title: Quiz Q#684 · J. M. Synge
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · J. M. Synge
items.stem: What sensational claim does the young fugitive Christy Mahon boast of that turns him into an instant folk hero in the Mayo village in The Playboy of the Western World?
options: That he robbed the British revenue garrison
That he escaped from a sinking prison barge
That he killed his tyrannical father with a loy (spade)
That he led an armed uprising against the bailiffs
items.explanation: The Mayo villagers idolize Christy for his daring patricide until his head-bandaged father Old Mahon arrives looking for him, exposing the gap between 'a gallous story and a dirty deed'.

items.title: Quiz Q#685 · J. M. Synge
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · J. M. Synge
items.stem: Which famous final line of bitter anguish is spoken by Pegeen Mike at the end of The Playboy of the Western World as Christy walks out with his father?
options: 'May the curse of the seven winds fall upon your house!'
'There is no man left in the county worth the price of a pint!'
'Let him go back to his cows and his digging, for I am wed to Shawn!'
'Oh my grief, I've lost him surely. I've lost the only Playboy of the Western World!'
items.explanation: Pegeen breaks out into wild lamentations realizing she has driven away the poetic hero she loved, left only with the sniveling Shawn Keogh.

items.title: Quiz Q#686 · J. M. Synge
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · J. M. Synge
items.stem: In J. M. Synge's one-act tragedy Riders to the Sea (1904), how many sons has the grieving mother Maurya lost to the relentless Atlantic Ocean by the play's end?
items.explanation: Maurya mourns her husband, father-in-law, and five sons already taken by the sea, before her final son Bartley is thrown by his grey pony into the waves and drowned.

items.title: Quiz Q#687 · J. M. Synge
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · J. M. Synge
items.stem: Which speech of sublime stoic resignation concludes J. M. Synge's Riders to the Sea?
options: 'The sea is a thief that neither priest nor prayer can bind.'
'They're all gone now, and there isn't anything more the sea can do to me.'
'We must weep for the young men while the tide turns dark.'
'God have mercy on the living, for the dead are peaceful.'
items.explanation: Maurya achieves classical tragic peace, sprinkling holy water over Bartley's corpse and declaring that she can now sleep without fear of the winter storms.

items.title: Quiz Q#688 · J. M. Synge
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · J. M. Synge
items.stem: In J. M. Synge's early comedy In the Shadow of the Glen (1903), what does the discontented Nora Burke choose to do when her husband Dan feigns death to catch her being unfaithful?
options: She shoots Dan with his own hunting rifle
She marries the young shepherd Michael Dara
She leaves the cottage to walk the roads with the Tramp
She drowns herself in the flooded glen
items.explanation: Nora rejects both her suspicious old husband and the timid Michael Dara, embracing the poetic freedom of the open road with the wandering Tramp.

items.title: Quiz Q#689 · J. M. Synge
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · J. M. Synge
items.stem: In the famous Preface to The Playboy of the Western World, what food metaphor did J. M. Synge use to describe how poetic dialogue should taste on the stage?
options: 'As fully flavoured as a nut or apple'
items.explanation: Synge famously wrote: 'On the stage one must have reality, and one must have joy... in a good play every speech should be as fully flavoured as a nut or apple'.

items.title: Quiz Q#690 · J. M. Synge
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · J. M. Synge
items.stem: Which Irish poet met J. M. Synge in a Latin Quarter garret in Paris in 1896 and famously advised him: 'Give up Paris... Go to the Aran Islands. Live there as if you were one of the people themselves'?
items.explanation: W. B. Yeats urged Synge to leave the Parisian literary cafes and immerse himself in the Gaelic culture of the Aran Islands, which sparked Synge's dramatic genius.

items.title: Quiz Q#691 · Samuel Beckett
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: Which Hungarian-British theatre critic coined the term 'The Theatre of the Absurd' in his influential 1961 study of Beckett, Ionesco, Adamov, and Genet?
items.explanation: Martin Esslin coined the term based on Albert Camus's philosophy in The Myth of Sisyphus to describe plays demonstrating the irrationality and meaninglessness of human existence.

items.title: Quiz Q#692 · Samuel Beckett
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: Which four-word philosophical statement of defeat opens Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot, spoken by Estragon as he struggles to pull off his boot?
items.explanation: Estragon's opening line—'Nothing to be done'—establishes the existential stalemate of human endeavor that permeates the entire play.

items.title: Quiz Q#693 · Samuel Beckett
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: What is the iconic, minimal stage setting specified by Samuel Beckett at the beginning of Waiting for Godot?
options: 'An empty room with two dustbins. Noon.'
items.explanation: Beckett's stage direction establishes the bare, universal landscape of existential waiting, with the lone tree sprouting four or five leaves in Act II.

items.title: Quiz Q#694 · Samuel Beckett
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: In Waiting for Godot, which subservient character delivers a torrent of breathless, unpunctuated academic gibberish when commanded by Pozzo to 'Think!'?
items.explanation: Lucky's extraordinary three-page monologue parodies theology, science, and scholastic philosophy, demonstrating the disintegration of human rationalism.

items.title: Quiz Q#695 · Samuel Beckett
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: How do both Act I and Act II of Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot conclude?
options: With Vladimir weeping beside the barren tree as darkness falls
With the dialogue 'Well, shall we go? / Yes, let's go.' followed by the stage direction '[They do not move]'
With the Boy returning to announce that Godot will definitely come today
With Pozzo and Lucky leading them away down the country road
items.explanation: The absolute contradiction between speech and action underscores the paralysis of the human will in an absurd universe.

items.title: Quiz Q#696 · Samuel Beckett
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: Which 1957 play by Samuel Beckett features the blind, wheelchair-bound protagonist Hamm and his limping servant Clov confined in a claustrophobic room with two high windows?
items.explanation: Endgame (Fin de partie) presents a post-apocalyptic endgame of human consciousness, named after the final stage of a chess match.

items.title: Quiz Q#697 · Samuel Beckett
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: Where do Hamm's elderly, legless parents, Nagg and Nell, live on stage throughout Samuel Beckett's Endgame?
items.explanation: Beckett visually materializes the discarding of the elderly and bodily decay by confining Nagg and Nell to trashcans, popping their heads out to ask for porridge.

items.title: Quiz Q#698 · Samuel Beckett
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: Which line opens Samuel Beckett's Endgame, spoken by Clov as he surveys the bare room and uncovers Hamm's chair?
options: 'Finished, it's finished, nearly finished, it must be nearly finished.'
'Can there be misery loftier than mine?'
items.explanation: Clov's opening monologue echoes Christ's dying words ('Consummatum est') while acknowledging that the lingering end never truly concludes.

items.title: Quiz Q#699 · Samuel Beckett
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: In Samuel Beckett's one-act monodrama Krapp's Last Tape (1958), how old is the protagonist Krapp as he listens to his younger self on a reel-to-reel tape recorder?
items.explanation: The elderly Krapp eats bananas and listens with bitter nostalgia and mockery to the tape he recorded thirty years earlier on his thirty-ninth birthday.

items.title: Quiz Q#700 · Samuel Beckett
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: In Krapp's Last Tape, which poignant memory recorded thirty years earlier does the aging Krapp obsessively rewind and play again?
options: His election to the Royal Irish Academy
The publication day of his first successful book
Drifting in a boat on a lake with a woman
His final farewell to his dying mother
items.explanation: Krapp replays the tender memory of lying together in a punt on the water: 'I lay down across her with my face in her breasts and my hand on her. We lay there without moving. But under us all was moving'.

items.title: Quiz Q#701 · Samuel Beckett
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: In Samuel Beckett's Happy Days (1961), what is the bizarre condition of the cheerful protagonist Winnie on stage?
options: She is tied to a rocking chair that rocks continuously
She is suspended in a glass cage above an empty stage
She is trapped inside an iron lung surrounded by newspapers
She is buried in a mound of scorched earth up to her waist in Act I and up to her neck in Act II
items.explanation: Winnie maintains relentless bourgeois optimism and combs her hair from her black bag while literally being swallowed alive by the earth under blazing light.

items.title: Quiz Q#702 · Samuel Beckett
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: Why did the Dublin-born Samuel Beckett deliberately choose to write his major works (including En attendant Godot and Fin de partie) in French before translating them into English?
options: To strip away poetic excess and write 'without style' in a foreign language
Because French censorship was more lenient than British licensing laws
To protest against British colonial rule in Ireland
Because his publisher insisted on a Paris-first release
items.explanation: Beckett explained that writing in French allowed him to escape the lush rhetoric and habitual idioms of his native English tongue, enforcing strict discipline and clarity.

items.title: Quiz Q#703 · T. S. Eliot
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: Which historical event is dramatized in T. S. Eliot's 1935 poetic drama Murder in the Cathedral, commissioned for the Canterbury Festival?
options: The 1535 execution of Sir Thomas More by Henry VIII
The 1170 assassination of Archbishop Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral
The trial and execution of King Charles I in 1649
The Gunpowder Plot to blow up Parliament in 1605
items.explanation: Murder in the Cathedral dramatizes Becket's return from French exile and his murder by four knights sent by King Henry II.

items.title: Quiz Q#704 · T. S. Eliot
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: In Murder in the Cathedral, which of the four Tempters offers Thomas Becket the subtlest and deadliest spiritual trap—seeking the glory of martyrdom out of pride?
items.explanation: The Fourth Tempter echoes Becket's own hidden thoughts, prompting his famous realization: 'The last temptation is the greatest treason: / To do the right deed for the wrong reason'.

items.title: Quiz Q#705 · T. S. Eliot
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: Who constitutes the tragic Chorus in T. S. Eliot's Murder in the Cathedral, giving voice to the fears and spiritual plight of the common people?
options: The Monks of Christ Church Priory
The Knights of the King's Council
items.explanation: The Chorus of ordinary working-class women of Canterbury bears witness to the martyrdom, longing to avoid catastrophe but ultimately consecrated by the sacrifice.

items.title: Quiz Q#706 · T. S. Eliot
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: Which modern psychological verse drama by T. S. Eliot (1949), modeled on Euripides's Alcestis, features the mysterious psychiatrist Sir Henry Harcourt-Reilly reconciling Edward and Lavinia Chamberlayne?
items.explanation: The Cocktail Party was Eliot's greatest commercial West End and Broadway theatrical triumph, blending drawing-room comedy with Christian sacrifice (Celia Coplestone).

items.title: Quiz Q#707 · T. S. Eliot
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: Which famous line opens Section I ('The Burial of the Dead') of T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922), overturning Chaucer's traditional celebration of spring?
options: 'Winter kept us warm, covering / Earth in forgetful snow'
'April is the cruellest month, breeding / Lilacs out of the dead land'
'Let us go then, you and I, / When the evening is spread out against the sky'
'Under the brown fog of a winter dawn, / A crowd flowed over London Bridge'
items.explanation: Eliot subverts the opening of The Canterbury Tales ('Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote'), presenting springtime renewal as painful to a spiritually numb world.

items.title: Quiz Q#708 · T. S. Eliot
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: In Section I of The Waste Land, which character is described as a 'famous clairvoyante' who possesses 'a wicked pack of cards' featuring the Drowned Phoenician Sailor and Belladonna?
items.explanation: Madame Sosostris's tarot card reading foreshadows the key symbolic motifs of the poem, including death by water and the dry sterile land.

items.title: Quiz Q#709 · T. S. Eliot
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: Which frantic tavern refrain repeatedly interrupts the Cockney dialogue between Lou and Bill about Lil's abortion in Section II ('A Game of Chess') of The Waste Land?
items.explanation: The London pub bartender's traditional closing call serves as an apocalyptic reminder of the urgent, fleeting nature of mortal time.

items.title: Quiz Q#710 · T. S. Eliot
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: Which ancient mythological figure is identified by T. S. Eliot in his Notes as the most important personage in The Waste Land, uniting all the other characters and watching the encounter between the typist and the young man carbuncular?
items.explanation: Eliot noted: 'Tiresias, although a mere spectator and not indeed a "character", is yet the most important personage in the poem, uniting all the rest'.

items.title: Quiz Q#711 · T. S. Eliot
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: What is the title of the briefest section (Section IV) of T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land, describing the fate of Phlebas the Phoenician?
items.explanation: Section IV, 'Death by Water' (translated in part from Eliot's French poem 'Dans le Restaurant'), meditates on mortality and the loss of worldly vanity beneath sea currents.

items.title: Quiz Q#712 · T. S. Eliot
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: In the final section of The Waste Land ('What the Thunder Said'), which sacred Upanishadic text provides the threefold thunder command: 'Datta. Dayadhvam. Damyata.'?
items.explanation: Eliot draws upon the fable of gods, men, and demons answering Prajapati's thunder in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad: Give, Sympathize, and Control.

items.title: Quiz Q#713 · T. S. Eliot
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: How did T. S. Eliot translate the final repeated Sanskrit blessing of The Waste Land ('Shantih shantih shantih') in his appended critical notes?
options: 'The Truth that shall set you free'
items.explanation: Eliot referenced Philippians 4:7, noting that 'Shantih' is the formal ending to an Upanishad equivalent to 'the Peace which passeth understanding'.

items.title: Quiz Q#714 · T. S. Eliot
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: Which late masterwork of religious and philosophical verse by T. S. Eliot, published as a unified book in 1943, consists of 'Burnt Norton', 'East Coker', 'The Dry Salvages', and 'Little Gidding'?
items.explanation: Four Quartets meditates on time, history, Christian mysticism, and the four classical elements (air, earth, water, fire), culminating in the Pentecostal imagery of Little Gidding.

items.title: Quiz Q#715 · W. B. Yeats
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: In W. B. Yeats's apocalyptic poem 'The Second Coming' (1920), which famous lines express the breakdown of social and moral order in the modern world?
options: 'The best lack all conviction, while the worst / Are full of passionate intensity'
'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold; / Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world'
'A terrible beauty is born / In the gray Dublin light'
'Now days are dragon-ridden, the nightmare / Rides upon sleep'
items.explanation: Yeats's prophetic lines capture the chaos following World War I, the Russian Revolution, and the Irish War of Independence.

items.title: Quiz Q#716 · W. B. Yeats
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: Which immortal opening line begins W. B. Yeats's celebrated meditation on aging, mortality, and art, 'Sailing to Byzantium' (1927)?
options: 'I have met them at close of day / Coming with vivid faces'
'Turning and turning in the widening gyre'
'That is no country for old men. The young / In one another's arms...'
'I walk through the long schoolroom questioning'
items.explanation: The poet turns his back on biological Ireland where mortal generations neglect 'monuments of unageing intellect' to sail toward the holy city of artifice, Byzantium.

items.title: Quiz Q#717 · W. B. Yeats
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: In 'Sailing to Byzantium', what does the aged speaker pray the 'sages standing in God's holy fire / As in the gold mosaic of a wall' to do?
options: 'Restore my youthful vigor and earthly joy'
'Carry my soul back to the green hills of Sligo'
'Silence the mocking birds that sing in trees'
'Consume my heart away; sick with desire / And fastened to a dying animal'
items.explanation: Yeats dramatizes the soul's agony trapped in a decaying physical body, begging to be gathered into 'the artifice of eternity'.

items.title: Quiz Q#718 · W. B. Yeats
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: What form does the speaker wish to take once out of nature at the conclusion of W. B. Yeats's 'Sailing to Byzantium'?
options: A golden bird fashioned by Grecian goldsmiths singing upon a golden bough
A silver salmon swimming in the mystic seas
A marble statue carved by Phidias
A holy monk illuminated in an ancient codex
items.explanation: The golden bird sings to the Emperor of Byzantium 'Of what is past, or passing, or to come', symbolizing pure, immortal aesthetic creation.

items.title: Quiz Q#719 · W. B. Yeats
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: Which famous refrain in W. B. Yeats's political elegy 'Easter 1916' registers the sudden transformation of ordinary Irish citizens into immortal tragic martyrs?
options: 'They shall be remembered for ever, / They shall be alive for ever.'
'All changed, changed utterly: / A terrible beauty is born.'
'Too long a sacrifice / Can make a stone of the heart.'
'The falcon cannot hear the falconer; / The centre cannot hold.'
items.explanation: Yeats reconciles his ambivalence toward armed rebellion with reverence for leaders like Pearse, MacDonagh, and Connolly who transformed Ireland through sacrifice.

items.title: Quiz Q#720 · W. B. Yeats
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: Which famous rhetorical question concludes W. B. Yeats's 1928 philosophical poem 'Among School Children'?
options: 'Did she put on his knowledge with his power?'
'How can we know the dancer from the dance?'
'Why should not old men be mad?'
items.explanation: The closing stanza uses the chestnut tree and the dancer to express an organic unity where form and life, art and artist, cannot be separated.

items.title: Quiz Q#721 · W. B. Yeats
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: In the sonnet 'Leda and the Swan' (1924), what historical catastrophe is ignited by Zeus's violent rape of the mortal girl Leda?
options: The destruction of Atlantis and the fall of Babylon
The Roman conquest of Britain and the burning of Rome
The Great Famine and the Easter Rising in Ireland
The Trojan War, the sacking of Troy, and the murder of Agamemnon
items.explanation: Yeats views the rape as the mythic catalyst that birthed Helen and Clytemnestra, initiating a new two-thousand-year classical cycle of historical violence.

items.title: Quiz Q#722 · W. B. Yeats
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: Which questioning couplet concludes W. B. Yeats's 'Leda and the Swan'?
options: 'Did she put on his knowledge with his power / Before the indifferent beak could let her drop?'
'How can we know the dancer from the dance / In such a wild, bewildering glance?'
'Was there another Troy for her to burn / Before the wheel of fate could turn?'
'What god has wrought this terrifying birth / Upon the helpless daughters of the earth?'
items.explanation: The closing question probes whether human consciousness can partake in divine purpose during moments of violent historical rupture.

items.title: Quiz Q#723 · W. B. Yeats
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: Which three-line epitaph, composed by W. B. Yeats in 'Under Ben Bulben', is carved onto his gravestone in Drumcliffe Churchyard, County Sligo?
options: 'Here lies a poet / Who dreamed for Ireland / And woke in glory.'
'Cast a cold eye / On life, on death. / Horseman, pass by!'
'A terrible beauty / In holy peace / At last doth lie.'
'Think where man's glory / Most begins and ends / And say my glory was I had such friends.'
items.explanation: Yeats's austere self-designed epitaph expresses aristocratic aloofness, heroic courage, and serene detachment in the face of mortality.

items.title: Quiz Q#724 · W. B. Yeats
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: What term did W. B. Yeats give to the collective unconscious reservoir of ancestral symbols and racial memories that inspires prophetic poetry in 'The Second Coming'?
items.explanation: Yeats believed that poetic visions emerge from Spiritus Mundi ('the Spirit of the World'), an occult universal storehouse of archetypal images.

items.title: Quiz Q#725 · Dylan Thomas
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: What strict nineteen-line poetic form, consisting of five tercets and a concluding quatrain with two recurring refrains, did Dylan Thomas use for 'Do not go gentle into that good night'?
items.explanation: The villanelle's rigid circular structure creates a relentless, urgent incantation as the refrains echo alternately across each stanza.

items.title: Quiz Q#726 · Dylan Thomas
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: In 'Do not go gentle into that good night', which four groups of men does Dylan Thomas catalog who rage against the dying of the light?
options: Wise men, good men, wild men, and grave men
Rich men, poor men, saintly men, and sinful men
Young men, old men, warrior men, and weary men
items.explanation: Thomas demonstrates that all men, regardless of their nature or wisdom, recognize at life's close how much remained unsaid or undone, fighting against death.

items.title: Quiz Q#727 · Dylan Thomas
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: For whom did Dylan Thomas compose the impassioned elegy 'Do not go gentle into that good night' as he confronted imminent blindness and death?
options: His close friend and patron, Vernon Watkins
His dying father, David John Thomas
The Welsh soldiers killed at Normandy
items.explanation: Thomas addresses his father in the final quatrain: 'And you, my father, there on the sad height, / Curse, bless, me now with your fierce tears, I pray'.

items.title: Quiz Q#728 · Dylan Thomas
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: Which lush, nostalgic lyric by Dylan Thomas celebrates his boyhood holidays at his aunt's dairy farm in Carmarthenshire, opening with 'Now as I was young and easy under the apple boughs'?
options: 'A Refusal to Mourn the Death, by Fire, of a Child in London'
items.explanation: 'Fern Hill' (1945) is Thomas's supreme pastoral ode, recreating the Edenic innocence and joy of childhood before the realization of time's dominion.

items.title: Quiz Q#729 · Dylan Thomas
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: Which famous paradox concludes Dylan Thomas's 'Fern Hill', expressing how childhood joy is secretly held captive by mortality?
options: 'The green fuse that drives the flower drives my red blood.'
'Death shall have no dominion in the holy earth.'
'We wake and weep under the sorrowing trees.'
'Time held me green and dying / Though I sang in my chains like the sea.'
items.explanation: The closing line masterfully unites the color green (youth, vitality) with dying, acknowledging that humanity is chained to time even in moments of greatest song.

items.title: Quiz Q#730 · Dylan Thomas
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: Which famous Dylan Thomas poem takes its title and central affirmation of immortality from Saint Paul's Epistle to the Romans (Romans 6:9)?
options: 'Before I knocked and flesh let enter'
items.explanation: Paul's biblical verse ('Knowing that Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him') inspires Thomas's vision of cosmic renewal.

items.title: Quiz Q#731 · Dylan Thomas
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: What is the name of the fictional Welsh coastal fishing village that serves as the setting for Dylan Thomas's celebrated radio drama Under Milk Wood (1954)?
items.explanation: Thomas playfully spelled 'bugger all' backwards to create the eccentric, dream-filled community of Llareggub.

items.title: Quiz Q#732 · Dylan Thomas
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: Which blind, retired sea captain serves as a central dreaming voice in Dylan Thomas's Under Milk Wood, reliving his voyages and dead shipmates?
items.explanation: Captain Cat sits at his window listening to the townsfolk's steps, dreaming of his drowned shipmates who visit him from the ocean bed.

items.title: Quiz Q#733 · Modernist Techniques
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Modernist Techniques
items.stem: How did Ezra Pound define an 'Image' in his seminal 1913 essay 'A Few Don'ts by an Imagiste' published in Poetry magazine?
options: 'A decorative photographic reproduction of natural beauty'
'A musical arrangement of metric syllables and rhymes'
'That which presents an intellectual and emotional complex in an instant of time'
items.explanation: Pound's definition emphasized psychological release and instantaneous perception, freeing poetry from Victorian verbosity and didactic moralism.

items.title: Quiz Q#734 · Modernist Techniques
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Modernist Techniques
items.stem: Which two-line poem by Ezra Pound stands as the supreme monument of the Imagist movement?
items.explanation: Written in 1913, 'The apparition of these faces in the crowd: / Petals on a wet, black bough' uses direct juxtaposition without any superfluous verb or adjective.

items.title: Quiz Q#735 · Modernist Techniques
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Modernist Techniques
items.stem: Which of the following was NOT one of the Three Principles of Imagism formulated by Ezra Pound, H. D., and Richard Aldington in 1912?
options: Direct treatment of the 'thing' whether subjective or objective
Adherence to regular iambic pentameter and symmetrical stanzaic rhyming
To use absolutely no word that does not contribute to the presentation
As regarding rhythm: to compose in the sequence of the musical phrase, not in sequence of a metronome
items.explanation: Imagists vigorously rejected rigid metronomic meters and conventional rhyme schemes in favor of free verse ('vers libre') shaped by the musical cadence of the phrase.

items.title: Quiz Q#736 · Modernist Techniques
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Modernist Techniques
items.stem: Which avant-garde visual and literary movement was founded in London in 1914 by Wyndham Lewis and Ezra Pound, launching the fiery, puce-colored journal BLAST?
items.explanation: Vorticism celebrated the dynamism of the machine age, viewing the vortex as 'that point in the cyclone where energy cuts nearest to the still center'.

items.title: Quiz Q#737 · Modernist Techniques
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Modernist Techniques
items.stem: In his 1923 review 'Ulysses, Order, and Myth', which critical term did T. S. Eliot coin to describe Joyce's technique of using ancient myth as a scaffolding to give shape to the futility of modern life?
items.explanation: Eliot declared that the mythical method was 'a step toward making the modern world possible for art', replacing the narrative method with mythic parallels.

items.title: Quiz Q#738 · Modernist Techniques
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Modernist Techniques
items.stem: Who coined the psychological term 'Stream of Consciousness' in The Principles of Psychology (1890), which was later applied to literary narrative by May Sinclair in 1918?
items.explanation: William James wrote that 'consciousness... does not appear to itself chopped up in bits... it is nothing jointed; it flows. A "river" or a "stream" are the metaphors by which it is most naturally described'.

items.title: Quiz Q#739 · Modernist Techniques
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Modernist Techniques
items.stem: Which British female novelist's thirteen-volume novel sequence Pilgrimage (1915–1938), centered on Miriam Henderson, pioneered stream-of-consciousness interiority before Joyce and Woolf?
items.explanation: May Sinclair first applied William James's term 'stream of consciousness' to literary criticism in 1918 specifically when reviewing Dorothy Richardson's Pilgrimage.

items.title: Quiz Q#740 · Modernist Techniques
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Modernist Techniques
items.stem: Why is the year 1922 universally designated as the 'Annus Mirabilis' (Miracle Year) of High Modernism in English literature?
options: Because the BBC was founded and British radio drama was born
Because W. B. Yeats received the Nobel Prize in Literature
Because it witnessed the landmark publications of James Joyce's Ulysses and T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land
Because Virginia Woolf published To the Lighthouse and A Room of One's Own
items.explanation: The simultaneous appearance of Ulysses (February 1922) and The Waste Land (October 1922), alongside Woolf's Jacob's Room, marked the definitive triumph of High Modernism.

items.title: Quiz Q#741 · Modernist Techniques
items.meta: The Modernist & Inter-War Era · Modernist Techniques
items.stem: Which British philosopher and critic's essay 'Romanticism and Classicism' (1911) famously predicted that 20th-century poetry would turn away from romantic infinite yearning toward 'accurate, dry, and definite' verse?
items.explanation: T. E. Hulme's rejection of Romanticism as 'spilt religion' and his championing of classical, hard, clear poetic form deeply influenced Ezra Pound and T. S. Eliot.
